Ellicott would render the opening not that the seventh month was come but that it approached, and notes that Tisri, answering to our September, was the most solemn month of the year, holding both the Day of Atonement and the Feast of Tabernacles; the phrase as one man he reads not as all of them but as with one consent. Gill agrees that the month was only drawing near, since the people had met and the altar had been built before its first day, and Delitzsch argues the same, adding that the altar must have been finished before the first day because the offerings began then. Henry fills in the journey, that they probably came from Babylon in the spring and must be allowed four months on the road, and makes the gathering voluntary: they came by agreement among themselves rather than by any command of authority. Though newly arrived in their cities with their hands full of providing for their families, such was their zeal that they left all their business to attend God's altar; and let worldly business be postponed to the business of religion, Henry adds, and it will prosper the better.

Clarke identifies Jeshua as the grandson of Seraiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar put to death, and the first high priest after the captivity, and explains why the altar came first: worship had to be kept up all the time the temple was in building. Ellicott puts it the other way round, that the altar was only the beginning of the work, the temple being as it were built around it as the centre of all. Henry draws two lessons: begin with God, and if we expect to be directed by his oracles let him be honoured by our offerings; and do what we can in the worship of God when we cannot do what we would, for they could not immediately have a temple but would not be without an altar, as Abraham built one wherever he came. On the setting of the altar the commentators diverge. Gill allows that the bases may have been those remaining from the old altar, and Clarke and Ellicott both take it for the old site, which Ellicott supposes was found among the ruins, so that all the new was signified to be a restoration of the old; Delitzsch rules the English out, holding that the Hebrew says upon its former place and not upon its bases, and that the marginal reading behind the plural is an incorrect revision.

That fear hastened them is agreed, though not what follows from it. Henry offers both readings, that though they were among enemies they built the altar anyway and would not be frightened from their religion, and that because they were in such danger they set it up, since apprehension of danger should stir us up to our duty, and we should let our fears drive us to our knees. Wesley takes the second and says they made the more haste lest they should be hindered. Ellicott reads the act politically as well, their first open defiance in the presence of the nations around, since until their offerings went up they did not feel sure of the divine protection, and near the altar they were strong. Henry notes that it does not appear they had fire from heaven, as Moses and Solomon had, but that common fire served them as it did the patriarchs, and that having begun they kept up the continual burnt offering morning and evening, having known by sad experience what it was to want the daily sacrifice. Wesley measures their zeal by their poverty: the law required much, but they offered more, for though they had little wealth they had much zeal, and happy are they who bring such a holy heat with them out of the furnace of affliction.
8:
Delitzsch reads the second year as that after their arrival from Babylon, and has Zerubbabel and Joshua begin by appointing the Levites from twenty years old upwards to the oversight of the building. Ellicott makes the same year the second of Cyrus and finds the month significant, Zif being the month in which Solomon laid the first foundation, while the Levites' commission and the age fixed for it stand in strict harmony with David's ordinances. Clarke accounts for the interval, spent clearing ground, felling timber, hewing and transporting stones. Henry presses the speed as zeal: they took little more than half a year over the preparations, so much were their hearts upon it, and when any good work is to be done it is wisdom to set about it quickly even where difficulty is foreseen, since so we engage ourselves to it and engage God for us. He adds that the work goes on well when magistrates, ministers and people are hearty and agree in their places to promote it, and that those who cannot work may still quicken those who do, as the Levites did, strengthening the workmen's hands with comfortable words.

On the names there is a textual difficulty. Wesley and Gill both warn that the Jeshua here is not the high priest but a Levite of the same name. Delitzsch counts three orders of Levites here and judges that the sons of Judah is a clerical error for the sons of Hodaviah; Ellicott leaves the reading standing, taking Jeshua and Kadmiel to be of the stock of Judah, or Hodaviah, as the two heads of Levitical families whose fewness was compensated by their unanimity and vigour. Delitzsch describes the ceremony: when the builders laid the foundation, the priests were set in their robes with trumpets and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the Lord after David's ordinance. Ellicott notes that everything goes back to earlier times, the offerings having followed the law of Moses and the music now following David's precedent, the trumpets belonging to the priests and the cymbals to the Levites by ancient ordinance; Gill with Ellicott explains the singing by course as responses taken by turns, one company answering another.

Henry hears in the hymn the one song never out of date, that God is good and his mercy endures for ever: let all the streams of mercy be traced up to the fountain, and the reviving of the church's interests, when they seemed dead, be ascribed to that mercy's continuance. Then the two cries. Those who knew only the misery of having no temple shouted at the sight of a foundation, to whom even this was as life from the dead, and we ought to be thankful for the beginnings of mercy before we have its perfection; those who remembered the first house wept. Why they wept is disputed. Wesley lists the poverty of the preparations, the absence of the ark and the Urim and Thummim, and foundation stones inferior in both size and cost; Clarke says the glory had departed, since even a grander house would still have wanted the ark, the heavenly fire, the mercy-seat and the spirit of prophecy; Ellicott nearly denies the comparison, holding that the weeping was not occasioned by any question of size or grandeur, unless they marked the smallness of the foundation stones, but by the great desolation measured against the past, while the younger men thought of the new future. Henry grants the tears some reason, since sin sullies the glory of any church, but calls it their infirmity to cast a damp on the common joy and despise the day of small things. Delitzsch corrects a misreading of the last verse: it does not say the weeping was drowned by the rejoicing, but that among the people too both cries were raised at once.
